text: Samson went to Gaza, and there he saw a prostitute and went in to her.
Word came to the men of Gaza: "Samson is here!" So they surrounded the place and lay in wait for him all night at the city gate. All night they kept still, saying, "At dawn we will kill him."

But Samson lay there only until midnight. At midnight he got up, took hold of the doors of the city gate and the two posts, tore them loose along with the bar, hoisted them onto his shoulders, and carried them to the top of the hill that faces Hebron.
Some time later he fell in love with a woman in the Valley of Sorek, whose name was Delilah.

The rulers of the Philistines came to her and said, "Coax him and find out where his great strength comes from and how we can overpower him, so we can tie him up and subdue him. Each of us will give you eleven hundred pieces of silver."
So Delilah said to Samson, "Tell me, where does your great strength come from, and how could you be tied up and subdued?"
Samson answered her, "If they tie me with seven fresh bowstrings that have not been dried, I will become weak and be like any other man."
So the rulers of the Philistines brought her seven fresh bowstrings that had not been dried, and she tied him with them.

With men lying in wait in the inner room, she called out to him, "Samson, the Philistines are upon you!" But he snapped the bowstrings as easily as a strand of yarn snaps when it touches fire. So the secret of his strength was not discovered.
Then Delilah said to Samson, "Look, you have made a fool of me and told me lies. Now tell me how you can be tied up."
He said to her, "If they tie me tight with new ropes that have never been used, I will become weak and be like any other man."

So Delilah took new ropes and tied him with them, and with men lying in wait in the inner room she called out to him, "Samson, the Philistines are upon you!" But he snapped the ropes off his arms like thread.

He said to her, "If you weave the seven braids of my head into the fabric on the loom." [Footnote: The Hebrew sentence breaks off here; ancient versions continue, "then I will become weak and be like any other man."]

versions.text: Then Delilah said to Samson, "All this time you have made a fool of me and told me lies. Tell me how you can be tied up." He said to her, "If you weave the seven braids of my head into the loom's web—"
versions.explanation: An em dash inside a quotation cannot be voiced in oral reading. A closed sentence with a footnote explaining the abrupt ending of the Hebrew reads more naturally aloud while still noting the textual situation.

text: So she fastened them with the pin and called out to him, "Samson, the Philistines are upon you!" He woke from his sleep and tore away the loom pin along with the woven fabric.

versions.text: So she fastened them with the pin and called out to him, "Samson, the Philistines are upon you!" He woke from his sleep and pulled out the pin, the loom, and the web.
versions.explanation: הַיְתַד הָאֶרֶג is a construct phrase, 'the pin of the loom,' not two separate objects; listing three items ('the pin, the loom, and the web') misrepresents the Hebrew and is confusing when read aloud.

text: Then she said to him, "How can you say, 'I love you,' when your heart is not with me? Three times now you have made a fool of me and have not told me where your great strength comes from."
She pressed him with her words day after day until he was worn out to the point of death.

So he told her everything in his heart: "No razor has ever touched my head, for I have been a Nazirite dedicated to God from my mother's womb. If I were shaved, my strength would leave me, and I would become weak and be like any other man."

When Delilah saw that he had told her everything in his heart, she sent word to the rulers of the Philistines: "Come up once more, for he has told me everything in his heart." So the rulers of the Philistines came to her, bringing the silver with them.
She lulled him to sleep on her lap, then called for a man, and she herself shaved off the seven braids of his head. Then she began to torment him, and his strength left him.

versions.text: She had him fall asleep on her lap, then called for a man to shave off the seven braids of his head. So she began to subdue him, and his strength left him.
versions.explanation: In the Hebrew the verb 'shaved' (וַתְּגַלַּח) is third-person feminine singular: Delilah herself does the shaving after summoning the man. The current wording assigns the act to the man, which reverses the agency of the Hebrew text.

versions.text: She had him fall asleep on her lap, then called for a man, and she shaved off the seven braids of his head. So she began to subdue him, and his strength left him.
versions.explanation: Adding "herself" makes the Hebrew agency of the feminine verb וַתְּגַלַּח unmistakable when read aloud, since the immediately preceding mention of "a man" can still be heard as the subject. "Lulled him to sleep" renders the causative וַתְּיַשְּׁנֵהוּ more idiomatically, and לְעַנּוֹתוֹ carries the sense of afflicting/tormenting rather than merely subduing.

text: Then she called, "Samson, the Philistines are upon you!" He woke from his sleep and thought, "I will go out as before and shake myself free." But he did not know that the LORD had left him.
The Philistines seized him, gouged out his eyes, and brought him down to Gaza. They bound him with bronze shackles and set him to grinding grain in the prison.
But the hair of his head began to grow back after it had been shaved.
Now the rulers of the Philistines gathered to offer a great sacrifice to their god Dagon and to celebrate, saying, "Our god has delivered Samson our enemy into our hands."
When the people saw him, they praised their god, saying, "Our god has delivered into our hands our enemy, the one who ravaged our land and multiplied our dead."
And when their hearts were merry, they said, "Bring out Samson to entertain us." So they called Samson from the prison, and he performed for them. They stood him between the pillars.
Samson said to the boy who was holding his hand, "Let go of me and let me feel the pillars that hold up the temple, so I can lean against them."

versions.text: Samson said to the boy who was leading him by the hand, "Let me feel the pillars that hold up the temple, so I can lean against them."
versions.explanation: The Hebrew has two requests: 'Let me be (release me)' and 'let me feel the pillars.' The first clause (הַנִּיחָה אוֹתִי) is missing. Also הַמַּחֲזִיק בְּיָדוֹ means 'holding his hand' rather than 'leading him by the hand.'

text: The temple was crowded with men and women; all the rulers of the Philistines were there, and on the roof were about three thousand men and women watching Samson perform.
Then Samson called out to the LORD: "Sovereign LORD, remember me. Please, God, strengthen me just once more, and let me with one blow take revenge on the Philistines for my two eyes."
Then Samson braced himself against the two central pillars on which the temple stood, his right hand on one and his left hand on the other,

And Samson said, "Let me die with the Philistines!" He pushed with all his might, and the temple came down on the rulers and all the people in it. So he killed many more when he died than while he lived.

versions.text: and Samson said, "Let me die with the Philistines!" He pushed with all his might, and the temple came down on the rulers and all the people in it. So he killed many more when he died than while he lived.
versions.explanation: The verse begins with a lowercase "and," which is awkward when the verse is read aloud or quoted on its own. Capitalizing keeps the sentence self-contained while preserving the narrative connective.

text: Then his brothers and his father's whole family came down, took him up, and buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol in the tomb of Manoah his father. He had judged Israel twenty years.

versions.text: Then his brothers and his father's whole family came down, carried him back, and buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol in the tomb of Manoah his father. He had judged Israel twenty years.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew has two verbs of motion in contrast: they "went down" (וַיֵּרְדוּ) and then "carried him up" (וַיַּעֲלוּ). "Carried him back" loses the up/down contrast that frames the burial journey.
